title: Consolidation playbook: LLM porting roadmap (OpenAI/Anthropic/Together -> Redwood)
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked HelixEdge through a migration roadmap for consolidating multiple LLM vendors to the Redwood API. Focus: API/response parity, cost/latency tradeoffs, private deployment options, and concrete pilot next steps. Customer is cautious about latency-sensitive scoring jobs and data residency / audit requirements.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-11-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 mins
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE); Priya Nair (Redwood SE); Miguel Torres (Product); Leah Brooks (Solutions); Daniel Park (HelixEdge); Rina Gupta (HelixEdge); Omar Khalid (HelixEdge); Tara Lin (HelixEdge)

Summary (auto): Quick demo of Redwood API and Console focused on migration from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together, discussion of Optimize recommendations for latency-sensitive scoring, and pilot scoping.

00:00 Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, i'll kick off and then pass to Priya for the technical bits
00:22 Daniel Park: yeah, thanks, Alex, quick context: HelixEdge runs a distributed scoring pipeline, we currently call OpenAI for generation and Together for a few classification models, and we're trying to consolidate to reduce vendor overhead and cut per-token costs
00:48 Priya Nair: perfect, we'll show the API parity map first — the goal is you shouldn't have to rewrite your whole client, just small adapter changes — then Console, and finally Optimize suggestions for batching/kv caching
01:12 Rina Gupta: to be explicit, three constraints: sub-200ms p95 on 256-token scoring (where possible), data residency for EU datasets, and full auditability for 6 months
01:38 Miguel Torres: noted — Redwood has Dedicated and Private options; Dedicated is our reserved capacity with SLA, Private lets you bring VPC and your KMS for keys
01:59 Tara Lin: and just to confirm, we're primarily concerned about parity of generated outputs for our existing prompt templates, not a model-retraining effort, right?
02:18 Alex Chen: correct, we're focusing on API/behavior parity — same prompts, same stop tokens, similar temperature/top-p, plus a mapping for model-specific quirks
02:37 Omar Khalid: security quick note — we need SSO/SAML, audit logs forwarded to our SIEM, and KMS integration. Also curious about encryption at rest for intermediate caches
02:58 Priya Nair: yep — SAML + SCIM is supported on the Console; audit logs can be streamed to your SIEM or exported; for key management we integrate with customer KMS for Private/Dedicated — caches in-memory on the serving nodes are encrypted and we can add disk encryption on Private installs
03:35 Alex Chen: i'll hand over to Priya to show a short parity mapping demo in the API with a Together python snippet to Redwood, then Console for routing rules
03:47 Priya Nair: (screen share) okay, snippet — here's a Together client call: model=wizard-13b, prompt=..., stop=["

"], max_tokens=512 — with Redwood you call /v1/generate, model param maps, stop tokens pass through, and we expose a compatibility layer for a lot of the common vendor options
04:18 Daniel Park: is conversation/state (kv cache) portable? our scoring reuses context between calls
04:34 Priya Nair: good question — KV cache semantics are similar; you can persist keys in the Redwood session layer or use our streaming token approach; for migration we often recommend an adapter that translates Together/Anthropic session IDs to Redwood session IDs, minimal app change
05:00 Rina Gupta: about latency — you said sub-200ms p95 on 256 tokens is a target, does that assume Dedicated? Hosted?
05:20 Priya Nair: for that SLO, Dedicated is recommended; with Hosted API you might see higher p95 depending on burst patterns, but Optimize can suggest continuous batching and prefix caching to hit your cost/latency sweet spot
05:44 Miguel Torres: Optimize will analyze token distribution and suggest kernel/quantization settings — e.g., int8 quant for 13b models typically saves tokens per-second cost with minor quality delta for scoring tasks
06:10 Daniel Park: okay, but our scoring is sensitive — small hallucinations break downstream rules. How do we ensure parity not just in latency but in deterministic outputs?
06:29 Priya Nair: deterministic behavior ties to seeding, temperature, and model architecture; our parity mapping includes a table of recommended settings per model family, plus a test harness you can run to compare outputs on your canonical prompt set
06:50 Tara Lin: can you show the Console route rules? we sometimes do routing by region and also by priority bucket (low-cost vs high-availability)
07:05 Priya Nair: sure — (Console demo) route policies can be by geo, cost tier, or fallback policy. e.g., primary: Dedicated eu-west, fallback: Hosted eu-west small; you can also weight traffic for gradual rollouts
07:38 Rina Gupta: do you support canary rollouts on model versions? we need to test a new quantized variant on 10% traffic before full roll forward
07:51 Priya Nair: yes — canary by percentage, canary by user cohort, and automatic rollback on quality regression if you attach eval sets in Console
08:12 Omar Khalid: about quality monitoring — we need alerts on regressions tied to specific prompt sets and to get diffs — does Redwood keep diffs of model outputs?
08:28 Miguel Torres: Console's evals store baseline outputs and will show token-level diffs and a regression score. You can set thresholds to trigger a rollback or to flag a human review
08:45 Daniel Park: sweet. now on cost: if we consolidate, what ballpark savings could we expect vs our current mix? we do a lot of 2k-token passages for summarization and 256-token scoring
09:05 Alex Chen: rough math — Optimize often finds 20-40% unit cost savings via batching, prefix caching, and quantized variants; for long contexts we can recommend model sharding or chunked scoring which lowers per-call cost
09:28 Rina Gupta: you mentioned prefix caching. how does that work with changing prompts? our prompts have a variable user query appended to a long system prompt
09:46 Priya Nair: we cache common system prefixes and reuse KV between similar prompts; if the variable part is short we still save a lot of compute. Optimize will surface hit-rate expectations so you know the ROI
10:10 Tara Lin: ok, let's talk about pilot scope — what minimal setup would you recommend to prove parity and perf?
10:24 Alex Chen: recommended pilot: 2 weeks of integration, we'll run dual-writing to your existing vendors and Redwood for a shadow mode; week 1 run parity comparisons on 3 canonical prompts, week 2 ramp traffic, measure p95/p99 and quality diffs; Redwood provides the test harness and reporting
10:47 Daniel Park: shadowing means we don't affect production? just comparison?
11:00 Priya Nair: yes — in shadow mode Redwood handles mirrored traffic and you can compare outputs offline; you can also run a percentage-based live test if you want a staged approach
11:19 Omar Khalid: for Private deployment, what does the network topology look like? we have strict egress rules
11:33 Miguel Torres: for Private we ship a control plane (managed) and a private data plane inside your VPC; no egress unless you allow it, and audit logs/KMS calls stay within your infra; we can support air-gapped for on-prem too but that's a longer path
11:58 Rina Gupta: any special certs or compliance packages needed for EU data?
12:08 Alex Chen: we have SOC 2 Type II; EU data residency is supported via dedicated eu-west regions and Private deployments can ensure logs and storage remain in-region
12:25 Tara Lin: can we get a short sketch of estimated costs for a 6-month pilot with dedicated small pool vs hosted credits?
12:38 Alex Chen: yes — i'll include a cost worksheet, but very top-level: hosted pilot with credits is lowest up-front; reserved Dedicated pool gives predictable throughput and is better if you want strict SLOs — i'll outline both in the follow-up
12:59 Daniel Park: (interrupt) what about model drift monitoring? we need to detect quality decay over time on live prompts
13:13 Miguel Torres: Console has continuous evals and can schedule periodic re-evals of sample sets; drift alerts can be configured per-route and per-prompt-set
13:29 Priya Nair: back to the code — here's a quick python snippet mapping OpenAI-style chat to Redwood's chat endpoint, small example of how to translate role/names and function-calls — (reads snippet) "messages=[{role:'system'...}]" — most apps only need a thin shim
13:55 Rina Gupta: function calling — our current flows use function-calling heavily to validate outputs, will Redwood support that pattern?
14:10 Priya Nair: yes, Redwood supports structured output and function calling; you'll map the JSON-schema the same way, works with the Console's tracing to correlate calls to responses for debugging
14:32 Daniel Park: latency again — if we keep using OpenAI for the most latency-sensitive path and move other workloads to Redwood, is hybrid routing feasible?
14:45 Alex Chen: totally — route by priority bucket. Use OpenAI for the ultra-low-latency lane, Redwood Dedicated for the steady high-volume lane, and a hosted fallback in other regions — the Console routes automatically
15:07 Tara Lin: good, that gives us flexibility. can you give an example of a tradeoff where cost wins over latency in your experience?
15:21 Priya Nair: for batch summarization where latency of a single call isn't critical, switching to a quantized variant with higher throughput and using continuous batching lowers unit cost significantly; for real-time chat you might keep FP16 on Dedicated
15:41 Omar Khalid: logging detail — we need token-level logs for audits, is that feasible while preserving PII protections?
15:54 Miguel Torres: we have token-level traces; for PII you can enable redaction rules in Console before logs are exported to SIEM, or route audit logs to an internal pipeline that performs redaction at ingestion
16:18 Daniel Park: let's talk conversion pitfalls — anything that bites teams often when they move from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together -> Redwood?
16:33 Priya Nair: two common things: 1) model name/param mismatches (e.g., temperature semantics slightly different), and 2) session management differences. We provide a parity matrix that documents recommended parameter transforms and a compatibility library to smooth transitions
16:56 Rina Gupta: does Redwood have client SDKs for Go and Java? our infra team prefers those languages
17:07 Alex Chen: yes — official SDKs for Python, Node, Go, and Java; and REST API so you can build low-level adapters too
17:27 Tara Lin: any gotchas for function calling schema validation across models? sometimes a model returns a field with a different type and our schema validations fail
17:45 Priya Nair: Console's evals will surface mismatches; we recommend strict schema enforcement on the client and a small tolerance layer that coerces types where appropriate — we can help set that up in the pilot
18:02 Miguel Torres: (notes) also worth highlighting: automatic fallback policies if a model variant fails, and routing to cheaper quantized variants if quality is acceptable
18:22 Daniel Park: do you have benchmarks for Together's wizard-13b to a Redwood 13b-quantized variant? any p95 numbers?
18:34 Priya Nair: we have internal baselines — typical p95 improvements with Dedicated + int8 are 15-30% vs standard hosted FP16 for similar models, but i'll run your exact workload to give precise numbers
18:54 Rina Gupta: ok, please run for our 256-token scoring and 2k summarization distributions
19:09 Priya Nair: noted, we'll include p50/p95/p99 plus cost per 1k tokens in the bench
19:24 Tara Lin: for the pilot, what data do you need from us besides prompts? any infra info?
19:36 Alex Chen: your infra diagram, egress rules, key rotation policy, and sample request rates. we'll also need a contact for SSO onboarding (Omar?)
19:48 Omar Khalid: yep, i'll own SSO/SAML and the compliance checklist
20:02 Daniel Park: small question — can Redwood run locally in our staging cluster for an offline evaluation?
20:15 Miguel Torres: short answer yes with Private on-prem package; we'd need to scope air-gap and resource requirements, usually a longer procurement cycle though
20:31 Rina Gupta: procurement — any standard terms for a pilot? trial credits usually?
20:42 Alex Chen: we do pilot agreements with credits for Hosted; for Dedicated pilots we do short-term reserved capacity with a ramp and cancellation clause — i'll pass legal the template
20:56 Tara Lin: are there any partners or SI vendors you recommend for helping with the infra setup? we sometimes use an infra consultancy for VPC networking
21:08 Miguel Torres: we partner with a few cloud infra SIs — i'll include introductions in the follow-up
21:20 Daniel Park: great. can we talk briefly about telemetry and observability? we need trace IDs tied to request IDs for end-to-end debugging
21:34 Priya Nair: the Console exposes request tracing, and you can forward trace IDs to your tracing system; token breakdown, route traces, and per-token latency are available per request
21:50 Rina Gupta: how long do you keep audit logs by default?
22:00 Alex Chen: default retention is 30 days for hosted, with paid options to extend to 6 months or longer; Private deployments can set retention as you control storage
22:18 Tara Lin: okay — rough timeline recap?
22:26 Alex Chen: propose: Nov 6 — parity spreadsheet and pricing; Nov 7 — HelixEdge provides prompt set; Nov 10 — Redwood runs bench; week of Nov 17 — pilot kickoff; two-week pilot, then evaluation report end of Nov
22:46 Daniel Park: sounds good. any blocker on our side for starting?
22:52 Omar Khalid: just need to confirm compliance list and get SSO details to you
23:04 Alex Chen: perfect. last quick q from me — are there internal stakeholders we should include in the pilot review?
23:14 Tara Lin: include product, infra, legal, and our MLOps lead — i'll loop them in the invite
23:26 Miguel Torres: (wrap) thanks everyone, we'll follow up with artifacts: parity matrix, pricing worksheet, pilot runbook, and bench plan
23:36 Daniel Park: thanks, appreciate the walkthrough
23:40 Rina Gupta: thanks all
23:42 End meeting

Notes: transcription contains a few mis-heard words and truncated phrases common to automatic transcripts. Some product names may be slightly off in the live audio capture.
